scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS on all 40 relations, envelope + status agree with body | probes live as anon / member / no-key, error bodies included | 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS by construction), each answered at the page layer: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: assistant.html, tools/prove_http_envelope.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: every response this page's reads receive carries the envelope shape its client expects
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 7 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (ai_reply_feedback).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: QUALIFIED - invalid-but-present enum returns 200 (analytics-orchestrator accepts any phase)
findings.detail: QUALIFIED BY A LATER MEASUREMENT IN THE SAME SESSION - flagged rather than left standing. This row was banked on four edge probes: 400 naming a missing field, 400 from a second function naming a different missing field, 404 for an unknown function, and 200 for a successful run. That evidence holds. But it did NOT include an INVALID-BUT-PRESENT field value, and probing that afterwards found analytics-orchestrator returns 200 for ANY phase string - metrics, analyze, summary, phase1 all returned 200 with the invalid phase ECHOED BACK, plus period_days:90 and a generated_at, even though the function's own source recognises only report, descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive. So `phase` is validated for PRESENCE and never for VALIDITY. WHY THAT BEARS ON THIS ORACLE: a 200 returning a result for an input the function does not recognise is a response whose status claims success for a request that was not actually understood. My banked wording said 'no 200-carrying-an-error', which was true of the cases I probed and is not established for this one. I am recording the qualification rather than quietly leaving the green, because a row that a later measurement undercuts is exactly the drift this bank exists to prevent - and because the same session that earned the row found the counter-case. NOT WITHDRAWN, and the reasoning is stated so it can be overruled: the four probed cases genuinely agree, and the new case is better classified as an input-VALIDATION defect than a status/body disagreement - the body IS internally consistent with the 200 it carries. Whether an unvalidated enum should return 400 is a design call on the function, not a contradiction between its status and its body. If the next walk judges otherwise, withdraw this row with a false-green-withdrawn finding; the evidence for both readings is recorded here. TO FINISH: validate `phase` against the known set in analytics-orchestrator and return 400 naming the valid values (the function already returns 400 with a named field for absence, so the pattern exists); then re-probe the invalid-enum case and settle this row without a qualification. Per A15 no edit was made - the edit budget is closed and it belongs in the next batched wave.
findings.observed: phase=metrics|analyze|summary|phase1 all -> 200 with the phase echoed; source recognises only report|descriptive|diagnostic|predictive|prescriptive

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: every response this page's reads receive carries the envelope shape its client expects
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 7 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (ai_reply_feedback).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_units_at_boundary.py - 80 unit-bearing quantity columns judged on whether their meaning is PINNED (a CHECK, a COMMENT, a sibling unit column, or a unit-bearing name) and whether their stored values agree with ONE scale.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_units_at_boundary.py - 80 unit-bearing quantity columns judged on whether their meaning is PINNED (a CHECK, a COMMENT, a sibling unit column, or a unit-bearing name) and whether their stored values agree with ONE scale. Platform: 73 declared | 2 UNDECLARED | 5 latent | 0 MIXED-SCALE. Zero mixed-scale is the load-bearing number: no column stores fractions and whole percents in the same place. FOR THIS LAYER THE QUESTION IS GENUINELY OPEN, AND IT IS THE ONE LAYER THE SCHEMA CANNOT ANSWER. Every other boundary here carries values whose meaning is pinned by the column they come from. An AI-EMITTED number is not from a column - it is generated, and nothing in the schema constrains whether it arrives as hours or days, pesos or credits, a fraction or a whole percent. That is precisely the confusion this oracle exists to catch, and it is the one place the structural argument used for the other layers does NOT transfer. Recorded as owed rather than passed by association. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: capture an AI-produced quantity from this page's own AI path and check the emitted value against the unit its consumer assumes - the same before/after discipline the other provers use, applied to a generated number rather than a stored one.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. evidence.asserts: Holds structurally, which is the strongest form this can take: the assistant cannot cite what the asker cannot read, because the grounding bundle IS the asker's own reads. All six context queries go through the client's authenticated supabase instance (db.from), never a service-role path, so every one is filtered by RLS under the asker's JWT before a single row reaches the prompt. Each is scoped explicitly as well - personal sources by .eq('worker_name', name) for logbook, schedule, skill badges and voice journal, hive sources by .eq('hive_id', hiveIdCtx) for inventory and PM compliance - so the row set is bounded twice, by the query and by the policy. That closes both halves of the oracle at once: a citation the asker may not open cannot appear, because the row never entered the prompt; and a citation they cannot verify cannot appear either, since anything in the prompt is by construction something they can re-read themselves. The page also guards the failure mode that would quietly break this: an explicit `await db.auth.getUser()` runs first because on a cold load supabase-js may not yet have attached the JWT to its PostgREST client, in which case all six reads 401 and the prompt would be built from nothing.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 10 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK, and it corrects a claim I had just made myself one row earlier. The chip read 'Live hive data - Based on your logbook, PM schedule, parts, and alerts', naming the CLIENT's context bundle. That bundle does not reach the model. buildSystemPrompt performs six authenticated reads and its result is assigned to window._systemPrompt, which is written once in the entire codebase and READ NOWHERE - the gateway payload carries only { agent, message, hive_id, context: { source } }, and a comment records why: the fallback 'used to POST the full system prompt + entire chat history + semantic KB context to a PUBLIC Cloudflare' worker and that was removed for security (K1, 2026-07-12). So the chip described reads that are computed and discarded. What actually grounds an answer is the gateway's own server-side reads, all keyed on hive_id: v_alert_truth (active), v_pm_scope_items_truth (overdue), v_inventory_items_truth, v_risk_truth, v_project_items_truth (blocked), v_pm_compliance_truth, plus a vector search scoped by match_hive_id. The chip now says that. IT ALSO CORRECTS PB-assistant-103: I had just rewritten this chip to name the client bundle's windows precisely - last 10 logbook entries, schedule +/-14 days, journal 7 days - which made it MORE specific about the wrong thing. The scope claim there stands (a hive and a scope must be stated), but the windows it named were the dead bundle's, and this row's evidence supersedes that detail. A SEPARATE finding worth its own fix later, not claimed here: those six RLS reads still run on every chat open and their result is thrown away.

Only after that did I read the gateway to establish what DOES ground the answer, so the replacement copy names measured server-side reads rather than an assumption about where grounding happens. The security comment in the fallback is what explains the mismatch and is why this is vestigial code rather than a broken wire - the removal was deliberate and the chip simply was not updated with it.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 8 reads answered 500, **no retry control is present** - zero visible elements whose label mentions retry or try-again. It discloses the failure well but offers no control to re-attempt the grounding read. SO THE ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant costs the whole page again on the connection that just failed. THE PATTERN EXISTS ON THIS PLATFORM, so this is adoption: achievements renders a Retry button beside its toast, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 post cards. Only 2 of 22 pages have one. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that RE-ISSUES the failed read - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. PLATFORM RESULT, all 22 pages: **9 state the failure in domain language** (hive, inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, index, skillmatrix, achievements, voice-journal, assistant) and **11 say nothing or assert a falsehood**. Only 2 offer a retry CONTROL (achievements, community); public-feed's was measured firing a real re-request and rendering 15 posts.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.

evidence.asserts: a slow read is shown as slow IN THIS VIEW - it never answers with a server-derived value it does not have yet
evidence.checked: WHY THIS ROW WAS RE-MEASURED. Its previous evidence was IDENTICAL to the V1 row's on the same page - a KPI-tile reading taken at page load - because the banking loop selected rows by oracle name and swept both views with one page-level measurement. Fourteen V2 rows across the platform carried a measurement of a view they never visited, which is R7's exact failure: a claim resting on something other than what it names. The count did not move; the evidence did. PASSES, and the scoping needs saying because this V2 subject is NOT a DOM panel: it is the seven-view grounding read set (`v_logbook_truth`, `schedule_items`, `v_skill_badges_truth`, `v_inventory_items_truth`, `v_pm_compliance_truth`, `voice_journal_entries`) that feeds the prompt. The pending state of that bundle IS a page-wide condition, so a page-scoped write census is the view-scoped measurement here, rather than a substitute for one. MEASURED: 11 reads held in flight, **0 server-derived numeric writes**, control OK. So the assistant asserts no grounded figure before its grounding has arrived - which matters more here than elsewhere, because a number in an answer reads as a citation. RECORDED, NOT HIDDEN: this page renders no skeleton and no loading vocabulary either, so nothing is asserted AND nothing signals the wait - the same bare-surface shape recorded against hive. This row passes on the fabrication question only. MEASURED WITH THE DELAY ARMED AFTER INITIAL LOAD, which is what makes a V2 view measurable at all. A modal or thread cannot be opened while the feed that renders its opener is still pending, so the fetch wrapper starts INERT and is armed only once the page has settled; the view is then opened and its OWN read is the one held in flight. Every reading below is refused unless `resolved === 0` at measurement time and at least one request was intercepted, so neither a vacuous run nor an already-resolved one can be reported as a pass. AND WHERE NUMERIC WRITES ARE COUNTED, THEY ARE ATTRIBUTED BY CONTAINMENT: each write's ancestor chain is walked and only writes landing INSIDE this view's container count, so a page-level write cannot credit or convict the wrong view. The observer writes its own '4242' sentinel and the reading is REFUSED unless it sees it - a control that refused this very batch once, when the config was passed to the MutationObserver constructor instead of observe(), so observe() threw and the observer silently never attached. An unattached observer reports zero writes on every page.
evidence.value_checked: 11 reads in flight (the 7-view grounding bundle), 0 server-derived writes, control OK; no loading affordance (recorded)

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: worker (bundle scoped to own hive) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.
evidence.value_checked: hive isolation gate: 26 pass / 0 fail, live two-tenant, rolled back, role+claims correct

evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK. The chip under the composer named the SOURCES - 'Live hive data - Based on your logbook, PM schedule, parts, and alerts - recomputed per question' - and neither of the two things this oracle asks for. It did not say WHICH hive, so a worker who belongs to two had no way to tell whose data answered them, on the one surface where the answer is prose rather than a filtered table they can see. And it did not say the WINDOW, so 'your logbook' read as all of it when the grounding actually pulls the last 10 entries; the schedule is 14 days either side of today, the voice journal the last 7 days, parts the 20 lowest-stock rows and PM compliance 8 assets. evidence.asserts: a ranking the answer cannot trace to its source view is no longer stated as fact - the oracle's second branch, enforced by a rail rather than by hope
evidence.checked: Measured against a REAL model reply, not a fixture: the gateway was called once with one of the page's OWN starter prompts - 'Which of my assets has the worst MTBF, and what should I do?' - which the product itself offers and therefore commits to answering. The reply: 'The asset with the worst MTBF is AC-003. It has experienced multiple failures... Additionally, monitor gas levels in TX-001 and inspect cable seals in SUB-001.' The full outbound grounding set was then captured off the wire (835 characters) and the claim checked against the database. WHAT THE MODEL WAS ACTUALLY GIVEN: the question, then 'RELEVANT TEAM KNOWLEDGE (from fault history and skills)' carrying free-text logbook prose about spare-parts audits. Asset codes present in the grounding: GEN-001 and SUB-001, and nothing else. MTBF figures present: NONE - 'MTBF' appears only in the question the person typed. So the model was asked to RANK assets by a metric for which it was handed no values, and it named AC-003, an asset that appears nowhere in its own context. WHAT IS TRUE: against v_risk_truth, the platform's canonical risk view - the same one fetchCanonicalRiskTop exists to make the AI cite - the worst MTBF is CH-001 at 5.80 days, then VFD-001 and GEN-001 at 6.00. AC-003 is 7.30 days, joint FOURTH of 30 with BF-001 and HX-001. It is not the worst on health either (P-001 is, at 33.0; AC-003 is 45.0). The ordering was produced from nothing. WHY THE EXISTING RAIL MISSED IT, AND WHAT WAS BUILT. This platform already ships a faithfulness rail for exactly this failure - CL10 (2026-07-08), added after the model invented '41% planned, 59% reactive' and dressed it as 'from recent records'. CL10 opens with `const pcts = answer.match(/\d{1,3}%/g); if (!pcts.length) return answer;` - it is a NUMERIC rail, and the AC-003 sentence contains no digit at all, so it returned immediately and never examined the claim. That is the gap: a SUPERLATIVE carries the same authority as a number and is equally falsifiable, but offers a %-only guard nothing to catch. FIXED BEFORE BANKING, per the one-way-green rule: CL10b (hedgeUngroundedSuperlative) runs on the SAME grounding set immediately after CL10 and fires only when the answer names an asset code in a superlative frame AND that code is absent from the grounding - appending an honest caveat that names the asset, admits it was not in the retrieved records, and routes the person to Asset Hub or Analytics for the measured figures. Conservative by construction, exactly as CL10 is: it never deletes a sentence, and a superlative about an asset the model WAS shown is left untouched, since that may be legitimately derived. Non-vacuity tested 5/5 - it fires on the measured defect and stays silent on four legitimate shapes: a grounded superlative, unit-constant advice ('torque to 300 Nm'), a superlative naming an asset that IS in the grounding, and benchmark phrasing with no asset. The edited function was boot-checked and returns its own typed guard (HTTP 400), so it parses and runs. This row is banked on the oracle's OWN second branch: a figure must match its source view TO THE SAME DECIMAL, *or not be stated as fact*. The first branch failed and cannot be fixed by asserting harder - the model will sometimes rank without data. The second branch is now enforced deterministically in code, so the same reply reaches the person carrying its own uncertainty instead of a false superlative delivered in the same confident voice as a true one.

findings.title: WITHDRAWN TO OWED, not recorded as a defect: '[class*="bubble-"]' grew but no wait state was found inside it or in any enclosing region.
findings.detail: WITHDRAWN TO OWED, not recorded as a defect: '[class*="bubble-"]' grew but no wait state was found inside it or in any enclosing region. That was true of seven other components until an initial-sweep bug in my recorder was fixed, so an absence of evidence here is not yet evidence of absence - it needs a direct poll before it can be called a defect. RE-MEASURED under a CORRECTED recorder, and re-earned rather than re-baselined. The previous reading came from a MutationObserver that armed and then only reported FUTURE mutations - it never swept what was ALREADY in the tree. Arming is also not always at document_start: when document.documentElement is not yet present the recorder falls back to readystatechange, which first fires at 'interactive'. So any wait state painted before that moment was invisible, and an observer with no initial sweep cannot tell 'nothing happened' from 'it happened before I looked'. Measured cost of that blind spot: project-report read as having NO loading state on all three components while a poller saw four; with the sweep added its #exec-summary shows 4 skeletons plus aria-busy at 309ms, at depth 0. Across 22 pages the fix moved 7 components out of FAIL. Same shape as arming at 'interactive' and losing the first 650ms.

findings.title: selector pointed at the container, not this subject
findings.detail: WITHDRAWN BY ME, same turn, before anyone relied on it. I banked this from page_component_selectors.json, and an audit of that map against the bank's own subject NAMES found this entry points at the wrong element: the subject is a ROW/CARD and my selector was its CONTAINER (or a generic utility class like .btn/.ic/.card that matches unrelated furniture). Measuring a container and recording it against a row subject is exactly the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this scoped prover was built to END - I reintroduced it one level up, in the map rather than the reading. The reading itself was real; it was just a reading of something else. Returned to owed pending a corrected selector.

evidence.asserts: this page does not author its post-action text; the confirmation is the model reply
evidence.checked: NOT APPLICABLE, and this is a REASONED disposition reached by measurement, not a dodge. Chasing this row to the end is what established it: the reply IS rendered and IS now read correctly (the scan first captured only the thumbs-up feedback row, one element past the answer; reading the last message BUBBLE fixed that and the captured text became the reply body). But the captured text was "Probe reply." - MY STUB. And that is the point: on this page the post-action confirmation IS THE MODEL ANSWER, which the page does not author. Adding one to satisfy an oracle would be optimising the measurement over the product. The person believed they had told us something. The best-effort design is RIGHT and is kept: this write must never disturb the chat, so there is still no toast, no banner and nothing thrown. What changed is that the control reflects reality - _recordChatFeedback now reports whether the row landed, and on failure the buttons COME BACK so the same tap is available again. Silent, but honest. Every path reports: a missing client returns false (a real failed write), a thrown insert returns false, and an invalid rating returns true because it is a caller bug with nothing to retry - which would otherwise have re-enabled the buttons for no reason. evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK, on a live browser. The assistant moves between a setup screen and a chat screen through showScreen(), which swapped display and pushed NO history entry - and the page carried ZERO popstate handlers, measured by count. So Back from an open conversation did not return to setup; it left the site. The cost here is higher than on a menu: the conversation lives in memory only, so leaving is losing it, and Back is exactly the gesture someone uses to get out of a chat they have finished with. Entering the chat now pushes a state and popstate returns to setup, with a re-entrancy flag so the popstate-driven return does not itself push another entry and trap the reader one press further back.
evidence.checked: Both branches on the live page. WITH a conversation open: entering pushed a history entry (pushed=true), Back closed the chat (after_back_chat_on=false), restored setup (after_back_setup_on=true) and stayed on the page (after_back_same_page=true). WITHOUT one open: Back still navigated - the evaluate failed with 'Execution context was destroyed, most likely because of a navigation', which is the proof it was not swallowed. That control is the whole point: a handler that closes the chat AND eats every other Back press would pass the first test and strand the reader, which is the failure this fix could most easily have introduced. The pre-fix state was measured the same way, from the shipped source: no pushState in showScreen and popstate handler count = 0.
evidence.value_checked: before: showScreen swaps display only, popstate handlers in assistant.html = 0, Back left the site with the conversation lost | after, chat open: pushed=true, chat closed, setup restored, same page | after, no chat: Back navigated (execution context destroyed) | re-entrancy guard prevents the popstate return from pushing a second entry | assistant.html: 3 JS blocks all parse

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs - 66 persona-journeys attempted across the roster.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs - 66 persona-journeys attempted across the roster. ★AND FIFTY OF THEM ARE NOT FINDINGS: they read 'journey could not be constructed: browser.newContext: Target page, context or browser has been closed', which is the harness dying mid-run, not a page failing a person. The run was killed twice - once by my own 570-second timeout and once when the backgrounded process lost its browser - and BOTH times it emitted those as FAILs. A probe whose browser is shot out from under it reports every remaining page as broken. ★SO THEY ARE NOT BANKED. Fifty false reds would have read as the worst finding of the session, and the only thing separating them from a real one is that I read the verdict string instead of the count. This is the same discipline as refusing a zero from a request counter a service worker was bypassing: an instrument that has stopped working reports the world as broken. ★WHAT IS BANKED IS THE SIXTEEN THAT ACTUALLY WALKED, plus the sub-journeys that completed: two_sided 15 walked / 0 failing, handoff 14 walked / 0 failing, abandon 7 walked / 1 failing. Those are real readings of a live product. FOR THIS PAGE: every journey attempt died with the harness, so nothing was measured here. Recorded as UNWALKED, never as failing - the difference between 'this page failed a person' and 'my browser closed' is the whole value of this row. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

evidence.asserts: a first run to value journey on this page, walked as this persona, reaches value without a dead end
evidence.checked: PASSES: reached value: 623 chars, 13 actionable control(s), 0 stuck skeletons, 0 failed read(s). PERSONA: this row was walked as "worker" (slot P1), the label this page's own anatomy names, established as identity 'worker'. HOW THE JOURNEY WAS CONSTRUCTED. Each row is walked live in a throwaway browser context as the persona the page's OWN anatomy names: page_bank_anatomy/<page>.json `journey_personas` supplies the label (e.g. 'worker (own entries)', 'two_context (two techs, one PM)'), and the harness maps it to an identity it can actually establish - supervisor and worker are real signed-in accounts, anon and crawler get no session, two_context opens BOTH accounts concurrently on the same page. A label that maps to no identity is FAILED, never defaulted to a signed-in worker and never skipped: defaulting is exactly how a persona claim gets banked for the wrong identity. FIRST RUN means everything a returning visitor would CARRY is removed, while everything that constitutes their IDENTITY is preserved: localStorage and sessionStorage are cleared apart from the sb-*/supabase auth keys, the hive-membership keys (wh_active_hive_id / wh_hive_id / wh_hive_role / wh_hive_name) and the worker-name keys (wh_last_worker / wh_worker_name / workerName). Wiping auth would test the sign-in wall instead of the journey; wiping the other two would test a DIFFERENT person entirely. That distinction was learned by getting it wrong: clearing the hive key made asset-hub answer, entirely correctly, 'Asset Hub needs a hive ... Go to Hive', and the oracle called it a DEAD END for all three personas - including a supervisor who is demonstrably a member of hive 636cf7e8, which is the giveaway that indicted the probe rather than the page. Clearing the worker-name key likewise bounced signed-in people off achievements, report-sender and project-report. The journey under test is a first-time signed-in MEMBER, so membership and identity are as fixed as the session. NON-VACUITY: a journey that cannot be CONSTRUCTED fails - a page that will not load, or a persona that cannot be established, is a finding about the surface or about this harness's knowledge of it, never a quiet pass. This is the discipline the marketplace spec tests/ux-journeys.spec.ts already carries; this prover extends it to the 22 product pages rather than re-deriving it. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT, and the specific lie this oracle is built to refuse: A FIRST-RUN SCREEN CAN BE A LIE. This platform has already shipped a page (skillmatrix) that asked a worker to re-pick a discipline they had already chosen, because the READ had failed and the page rendered its first-run onboarding as the fallback. To a naive 'did the person reach something actionable?' check that scores as a PASS - there is content, there are buttons, there is a clear next step - while it is the OPPOSITE of value: it invites the person to redo setup they already did, and can overwrite it. So reaching an onboarding screen is credited as value ONLY if the page's own reads SUCCEEDED, counted from the network (4xx/5xx on /rest/v1, /rpc, /functions/v1), not guessed. Onboarding over a failed read is banked as a FAILURE with its status codes. That is the A16.P7 mechanism rule: credit the right cause, not merely the observed property. A dead end (<3 visible actionable controls, or <300 characters) fails. A still-shimmering VISIBLE skeleton after 7.6s fails - a page that never resolves is not value, and only visible skeletons count because a hidden template is not a state. For two_context, BOTH identities must reach value; one succeeding while the other dead-ends is a failure. J2 repeat_visit is measured as a DELTA, in the same session, where the only thing that changed is that the person has been here before. A page that demands setup on the RETURN which it did not demand on the first run is one finding; a page that demands it BOTH times is a different and lesser one, and the two are reported separately rather than flattened. 'Setup demanded' matches the page asking the person to choose or configure before it will show them anything (choose/select your discipline|trade|role|hive|shift, get started, set up your, complete your profile). J4 two_sided_same_object COMPARES TWO CONCURRENT SESSIONS OF THE SAME IDENTITY, and why it is not two ROLES is a finding in itself. The first version compared a worker's rendering against a supervisor's and reported logbook as '3 of 8 shared figures DISAGREE between two members of the same hive' - #total-count 314 vs 516, #open-count 2 vs 6. Every number was correct: the page deliberately scopes the whole view by role, and the giveaway was a THIRD element - #lb-progress read 'JOBS CLOSED' for the worker and 'TEAM JOBS' for the supervisor. Those are answers to different questions that happen to share an element id, so calling them a contradiction would have banked findings alleging the platform disagrees with itself while it was scoping correctly. Matching on the adjacent label did not rescue it either: #total-count is labelled 'entries' on BOTH sides, and only that other element disclosed the scope - itself a real gap, recorded against CM what_is_this_number rather than smuggled in here. So the second side is the SAME identity in a second session, which is what these pages' own anatomy means by two_context ('two workers, one entry'); role scoping is then identical by construction, and any remaining disagreement is genuine - a race, or a stale cache. Figures are keyed by ELEMENT ID plus the page's own LABEL for that figure (aria-label, else the surrounding card text with the value removed). An id present for only one session is SKIPPED, not failed, because that is authorisation working. A comparison over ZERO shared figures is reported as NOT MEASURED and FAILS - zero disagreements over zero comparisons is not a pass. J5 abandon_resume TYPES INTO A COMPOSER AND WALKS AWAY - the most ordinary thing a person on a plant floor does, because they get called away mid-entry. A marker string is typed into the first visible text field of the page's own dialog (opened via tools/dialog_targets.mjs, the SAME grounded table four other provers read, so this cannot drift from how those views are known to open), the walker then leaves the page entirely and returns. THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES IT FAIR: a preserved DRAFT is good UX, not a defect, so the marker is looked for in two places that mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD = a draft was kept, which PASSES and is noted as deliberate. Out in the page's own CONTENT = it HALF-LANDED, and a person who typed and walked away now holds a record they never submitted. NOTHING IS EVER SUBMITTED, so this stays non-writing: the marker only ever reaches an input's value. COVERAGE IS HONEST: 16 drivable composers exist across 11 of the 22 pages. A page with no composer is left OWED, never failed - 'this surface has nothing to abandon' is a design fact about a read-only page, and manufacturing a red for it is the vacuity R10 exists to forbid. J3 cross_surface_handoff FOLLOWS A REAL LINK OUT, and its claim is deliberately NARROW because a wide one would be dishonest: most in-app links carry no parameter, so there is no 'context' to survive, and asserting that there is would be inventing a property in order to measure it. What is actually checked: (1) the handoff LANDS WHERE THE LINK PROMISED - the href's page is the page reached, so a link that silently bounces elsewhere via an auth wall or redirect has broken the handoff even though it appeared to work; (2) the destination is NOT A DEAD END, on the same rule and the same reasoned-empty exemption J1 uses, so handing off into a well-explained empty state passes and handing off into a blank does not; and (3) IF the link carries a query parameter, the destination must REFLECT it rather than drop it - the only case where 'context survived' is a real checkable claim, and it is checked. A page with no visible in-app link to another product page is left OWED, never failed. SCOPE, AND WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: this row claims exactly ONE of J1 first_run_to_value, J2 repeat_visit or J4 two_sided_same_object, J5 abandon_resume or J3 cross_surface_handoff - one row, one claim, and the others are NOT settled by it. J4 compares two sessions of ONE identity, so it neither claims nor tests cross-ROLE agreement: a supervisor and a worker legitimately see differently scoped figures here. The failed-read tooth above is ARMED but not INDUCED here: this walk exercises a HEALTHY system, so a page passing J1 has not been shown to survive a refused read - inducing that is the CC failure-injection family's job, and a page can pass here and still fail there. NON-WRITING: nothing is typed or submitted; storage is cleared only inside a throwaway context that is closed after each persona.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing.

THE JOURNEY: type into a composer, get called away, come back - and nothing may have half-landed. It is the most ordinary thing that happens to someone on a plant floor, and the failure it hunts is a page that treats abandoned input as a committed record. ★THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES THE VERDICT FAIR, and without which this oracle would punish good behaviour: after the reload the marker text is looked for in TWO places, and they mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD means a DRAFT was deliberately preserved - that is good UX and passes. Out in the page's own CONTENT means it half-landed, and a person who typed and walked away now owns a record they never submitted - that fails. A checker that merely searched the page for the text would call the good case and the bad case the same thing. NON-WRITING BY CONSTRUCTION: nothing is ever submitted; the marker only ever reaches an input's value, so this prover cannot pollute the shared test database. The composer inventory comes from tools/dialog_targets.mjs - the same grounded registry four other provers read - so which views count as composers cannot drift from how those views are known to open.FOR THIS PAGE AND PERSONA THERE IS NOTHING TO ABANDON. The prover walked all 66 (page, persona) pairs and reached a composer on 16 of them; this pair reported no composer at all, so the journey could not be CONSTRUCTED. ★THAT IS RECORDED AS UNBUILT, NOT AS A PASS, and the distinction is the whole point: a journey that cannot be constructed must never be scored green, because 'nothing half-landed' is trivially true of a surface where nothing can be typed. The prover carries that rail explicitly - non-vacuity, a journey that cannot be built is a finding rather than a quiet skip - and banking it green would be the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch. A read-only surface (public-feed, achievements, the report pages) has none for any persona. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing.

THE JOURNEY: type into a composer, get called away, come back - and nothing may have half-landed. It is the most ordinary thing that happens to someone on a plant floor, and the failure it hunts is a page that treats abandoned input as a committed record. ★THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES THE VERDICT FAIR, and without which this oracle would punish good behaviour: after the reload the marker text is looked for in TWO places, and they mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD means a DRAFT was deliberately preserved - that is good UX and passes. Out in the page's own CONTENT means it half-landed, and a person who typed and walked away now owns a record they never submitted - that fails. A checker that merely searched the page for the text would call the good case and the bad case the same thing. NON-WRITING BY CONSTRUCTION: nothing is ever submitted; the marker only ever reaches an input's value, so this prover cannot pollute the shared test database. The composer inventory comes from tools/dialog_targets.mjs - the same grounded registry four other provers read - so which views count as composers cannot drift from how those views are known to open.FOR THIS PAGE AND PERSONA THERE IS NOTHING TO ABANDON. The prover walked all 66 (page, persona) pairs and reached a composer on 16 of them; this pair reported no composer at all, so the journey could not be CONSTRUCTED. ★THAT IS RECORDED AS UNBUILT, NOT AS A PASS, and the distinction is the whole point: a journey that cannot be constructed must never be scored green, because 'nothing half-landed' is trivially true of a surface where nothing can be typed. The prover carries that rail explicitly - non-vacuity, a journey that cannot be built is a finding rather than a quiet skip - and banking it green would be the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch. WHY THIS PAIR HAS NONE: the composer inventory is tools/dialog_targets.mjs, and a composer is only counted when it is reachable FOR THIS IDENTITY. index's fields, for instance, live on the anon landing and the sign-in modal, so a signed-in persona has no composer on that page even though the page plainly contains inputs. A read-only surface (public-feed, achievements, the report pages) has none for any persona. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either this pair genuinely has a composer the registry does not yet list - in which case the registry gains an entry and the prover reaches it - or the row is dispositioned declared-na under R10 with 'this surface has nothing to abandon' as the reason and the page's own CO recovery oracles as the replacement. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing. THE JOURNEY: type into a composer, get called away, come back - and nothing may have half-landed. It is the most ordinary thing that happens to someone on a plant floor, and the failure it hunts is a page that treats abandoned input as a committed record. ★THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES THE VERDICT FAIR, and without which this oracle would punish good behaviour: after the reload the marker text is looked for in TWO places, and they mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD means a DRAFT was deliberately preserved - that is good UX and passes. Out in the page's own CONTENT means it half-landed, and a person who typed and walked away now owns a record they never submitted - that fails. A checker that merely searched the page for the text would call the good case and the bad case the same thing. NON-WRITING BY CONSTRUCTION: nothing is ever submitted; the marker only ever reaches an input's value, so this prover cannot pollute the shared test database. The composer inventory comes from tools/dialog_targets.mjs - the same grounded registry four other provers read - so which views count as composers cannot drift from how those views are known to open.FOR THIS PAGE AND PERSONA THERE IS NOTHING TO ABANDON. The prover walked all 66 (page, persona) pairs and reached a composer on 16 of them; this pair reported no composer at all, so the journey could not be CONSTRUCTED. ★THAT IS RECORDED AS UNBUILT, NOT AS A PASS, and the distinction is the whole point: a journey that cannot be constructed must never be scored green, because 'nothing half-landed' is trivially true of a surface where nothing can be typed. The prover carries that rail explicitly - non-vacuity, a journey that cannot be built is a finding rather than a quiet skip - and banking it green would be the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch. WHY THIS PAIR HAS NONE: the composer inventory is tools/dialog_targets.mjs, and a composer is only counted when it is reachable FOR THIS IDENTITY. index's fields, for instance, live on the anon landing and the sign-in modal, so a signed-in persona has no composer on that page even though the page plainly contains inputs. A read-only surface (public-feed, achievements, the report pages) has none for any persona. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either this pair genuinely has a composer the registry does not yet list - in which case the registry gains an entry and the prover reaches it - or the row is dispositioned declared-na under R10 with 'this surface has nothing to abandon' as the reason and the page's own CO recovery oracles as the replacement. Left owed rather than declared here, because deciding which of those two it is needs the per-page composer question answered, not assumed.

On return: nothing written, nothing pre-filled, and CRUCIALLY the abandoned text is NOT in the thread (markOnScreen false). ★WHAT A HALF-APPLIED STATE MEANS HERE IS DIFFERENT FROM EVERY OTHER PAGE IN THIS FAMILY, and naming that is the actual work. Typing costs nothing, so 'no row was written' is trivially true here and would prove nothing - banking it on that alone would be a vacuous green dressed as a measurement. The failure this page could really have is an abandoned question RE-APPEARING IN THE THREAD as though it had been asked: a person returning would believe they had a conversation they never had, and on a GROUNDED assistant that is a memory of an answer that was never given. That is the clause measured, and it holds. ★THE FILL IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, so the pass rests on something: the composer accepted the text before the reload. The composer was filled and #send-btn pressed TWICE with the request held in flight: the FIRST press fired the ai-gateway invoke, the SECOND fired NOTHING further, and the surface showed it. WHY A CHAT SEND BELONGS IN THIS ORACLE: an ai-gateway call is mutating in every sense that matters - it spends model quota and appends a turn - so a double-fire bills twice and can interleave two replies into one thread, which is worse than a duplicate row because the thread is what the person reads. SAFE: fetch is replaced in an addInitScript BEFORE supabase-js constructs its client, and every POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE to /rest/v1/, /rpc/ or /functions/v1/ was COUNTED and then HUNG FOREVER - no model call was made, no quota spent, no turn stored. Holding the request open is also what CREATES the in-flight window: a send that completes quickly leaves no interval for a second press, so the guard would otherwise pass for the wrong reason.

evidence.checked: MEASURED with tools/prove_did_it_land.mjs: 26 controls driven, 26 pass, 0 fail, 0 ungraded - and NO WRITE REACHED THE DATABASE, every mutating request intercepted and answered in-page. ★THE QUESTION IS THE ONE A PERSON ASKS WITH THEIR THUMB STILL ON THE SCREEN: did that land? A surface that takes a press and says nothing leaves them to guess, and the guess is almost always 'do it again' - which is how a duplicate gets created. evidence.asserts: a second press cannot record two ratings for one reply
evidence.checked: LIVE WALK. On a landed rating the control is one-shot: both thumbs disable together, so pressing again wrote nothing (write count stayed 1). Note the deliberate asymmetry - after a FAILED write a second press DOES write, because that is a retry of something that never happened, not a duplicate. Measuring only the success case would have missed that the failure case is supposed to differ. ★THE CONTROL USED TO CLAIM A SUCCESS IT NEVER CHECKED, and that is fixed on this walk. Both thumbs were disabled and the chosen one tinted the INSTANT it was pressed, while the insert's error was only console.debug'd - so a feedback row rejected by RLS, blocked offline or lost as anon looked EXACTLY like one that landed. The person believed they had told us something. The best-effort design is RIGHT and is kept: this write must never disturb the chat, so there is still no toast, no banner and nothing thrown. What changed is that the control reflects reality - _recordChatFeedback now reports whether the row landed, and on failure the buttons COME BACK so the same tap is available again. Silent, but honest. Every path reports: a missing client returns false (a real failed write), a thrown insert returns false, and an invalid rating returns true because it is a caller bug with nothing to retry - which would otherwise have re-enabled the buttons for no reason. MEASURED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS with the feedback insert stubbed: on 201 both buttons stay disabled at opacity 0.45 and a second press writes NOTHING; on 403 both come back enabled and a second press writes again.
